font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">That's an excellent neuroanatomical question. 👆</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">The apparent "paradox" you've identified — right hemiparesis with a right UMN facial palsy from a pontine lesion — actually makes perfect anatomical sense when you distinguish **where** in the pons the lesion sits: **ventral (basis pontis) vs. dorsal (tegmentum).**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">---</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">**THE TWO PONTINE SYNDROMES — WHY THEY DIFFER**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">**1. Millard-Gubler (Ventral Pontine Tegmentum Lesion) — the "classic" you're taught:**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Lesion in the **dorsal/tegmental** pons.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Hits the **corticospinal tract** → contralateral hemiparesis.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Hits the **exiting facial nerve fascicles** (after they loop around CN VI nucleus, before they exit the pontomedullary junction) → **ipsilateral LMN facial palsy.**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Offending side: LEFT pons → RIGHT hemiparesis + LEFT LMN facial palsy.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">Why LMN? Because the facial nerve fascicles have already left the facial nucleus — you're hitting the peripheral nerve fibers themselves, producing a complete ipsilateral facial droop (forehead included).</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">---</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">**2. Basis Pontis Lesion (Pure Motor Tract) — THIS PATIENT'S PATTERN:**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Lesion confined to the **ventral pons (basis pontis)** — the territory of descending white matter tracts.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Hits the **corticospinal tract** → contralateral hemiparesis.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Hits the **corticobulbar fibers** destined for the facial nucleus — these fibers run with the corticospinals and **have not yet decussated** at this level.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">- Offending side: LEFT basis pontis → **RIGHT hemiparesis + RIGHT UMN facial palsy.**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">Why UMN and ipsilateral to the hemiparesis? Because the corticobulbar fibers to the facial nucleus are still ipsilateral at the pontine level — they haven't crossed yet. A left pontine lesion knocks out the motor commands heading to the right facial nucleus. The facial nucleus itself and its exiting axons (in the tegmentum) are completely spared. The result is a **contralateral UMN-type facial weakness** — sparing the forehead (bilateral UMN innervation to the upper face) but weakening the lower face.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">---</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">**WHY THIS FITS OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION (CPM)**</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">This is the signature of **Central Pontine Myelinolysis** — osmotic demyelination preferentially affects the **central pons and basis pontis**, where the transverse pontocerebellar fibers and densely packed descending motor tracts create a vulnerable osmotic microenvironment. The tegmentum (housing CN nuclei and exiting fibers) is relatively spared early on. That's exactly why you get a "pure motor tract" syndrome: contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral UMN facial palsy — an UMN-on-UMN pattern with **same-sided deficits**, not crossed.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">---</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;">**In summary:** The lesion is in the left basis pontis. Corticospinal + corticobulbar fibers are both still ipsilateral at this level and both go to the contralateral side. Both are hit before decussation. Right-sided UMN hemiparesis + right UMN facial palsy. No LMN component because the tegmentum is spared. That's ODS, not Millard-Gubler.</p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; font-family: &quot;google sans flex&quot;, &quot;google sans&quot;, &quot;helvetica neue&quot;, sans-serif; font-size: medium; margin: 0px;"><br /></p><p style="color: #1f1f1f; letter-spacing: 0px; line-height: 1.25rem; margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; min-width: 0px; white-space-collapse: collapse;">Descending Course of the Corticospinal Tract through the Basis Pontis.&nbsp;Source:&nbsp;VectorMine / Getty Images</div></div></div></div><h2 style="margin-bottom: 0px;">The Neuroanatomical Cross-Section: Tegmentum vs. Basis Pontis</h2><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;">Think of a cross-section of the middle-to-lower pons divided into two distinct functional zones by an imaginary horizontal line:</p><div style="border-radius: 12px; margin: 16px 0px;"><div style="padding: 26px 0px 32px 32px;"><pre style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; text-wrap: wrap;"><code style="background-color: transparent; border-radius: 12px; direction: ltr; display: block; font-family: &quot;google sans code&quot;, monospace; font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-size: 0.875rem; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; line-height: 1.3125rem; padding: 0px;"> [ DORSAL / POSTERIOR ] +-----------------------------<wbr></wbr>------------------------------<wbr></wbr>----+ | PONTINE TEGMENTUM | | * CN VII (Facial) Nucleus * CN VI (Abducens) Nucleus | | * Exiting CN VII Fascicles * Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus| +=============================<wbr></wbr>==============================<wbr></wbr>====+ &lt;-- Boundary line | BASIS PONTIS | | * Corticospinal Tracts (descending motor to limbs) | | * Corticobulbar Tracts (descending UMNs to CN nuclei) | +-----------------------------<wbr></wbr>------------------------------<wbr></wbr>----+ [ VENTRAL / ANTERIOR ] </code></pre></div></div><h2 style="margin-bottom: 0px;">Tracing the Two Distinct Pathologies</h2><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;">By visualizing this cross-section, we can see exactly why the patient's presentation points directly to the basis pontis (as seen in Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome/CPM) rather than the dorsal tegmentum (Millard-Gubler Syndrome).</p><h3>Scenario A: Millard-Gubler Syndrome (Dorsal Tegmental Lesion)</h3><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;">When a lesion occurs dorsally in the <span style="font-weight: 700;">tegmentum</span>, it strikes the structures after the motor commands have already split or processed:</p><ul style="list-style-type: none; margin: 0px;"><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">CN VII Fascicles:</span> The lower motor neuron (LMN) fibers traveling outward from the facial nucleus are obliterated. Because these fibers supply the ipsilateral side of the face entirely, you see a full <span style="font-weight: 700;">ipsilateral LMN facial palsy</span> (inability to smile or wrinkle the forehead on the side of the lesion).</p></li><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">Corticospinal Ventral Extension:</span> If the lesion is large enough to extend slightly ventral or involve adjacent tracts, it catches the corticospinal fibers before they cross in the medulla, leading to a <span style="font-weight: 700;">contralateral hemiparesis</span>.</p></li><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">Result:</span> Alternating/crossed hemiplegia (e.g., Left brainstem lesion = Left face drop + Right body weakness).</p></li></ul><h3>Scenario B: Pure Basis Pontis Lesion (The Patient's Pattern)</h3><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;">In Central Pontine Myelinolysis, the demyelination preferentially targets the fat, densely packed tracts running through the ventral <span style="font-weight: 700;">basis pontis</span>. The dorsal tegmentum remains completely untouched.</p><div style="border-radius: 12px; margin: 16px 0px;"><div style="padding: 26px 0px 32px 32px;"><pre style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; text-wrap: wrap;"><code style="background-color: transparent; border-radius: 12px; direction: ltr; display: block; font-family: &quot;google sans code&quot;, monospace; font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-size: 0.875rem; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; line-height: 1.3125rem; padding: 0px;"> LEFT BASIS PONTIS LESION EFFECT ON THE BODY +-----------------------------<wbr></wbr>-----+ +--------------------------+ | [Corticospinal Tract] | | RIGHT SIDE OF THE BODY | | Caught BEFORE medullary | ---&gt;| Hemiparesis/Spasticity | | decussation | | (Contralateral) | +-----------------------------<wbr></wbr>-----+ +--------------------------+ | [Corticobulbar Tract] | | RIGHT LOWER FACE | | Caught BEFORE crossing to the | ---&gt;| UMN Facial Palsy | | right CN VII nucleus | | (Forehead Spared) | +-----------------------------<wbr></wbr>-----+ +--------------------------+ </code></pre></div></div><ol start="1" style="margin: 0px;"><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">The Corticobulbar Fiber Trajectory:</span> Upper motor neurons destined for the facial nucleus travel in the corticobulbar tract alongside the corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis. At this horizontal level of the left pons, the fibers meant for the right facial nucleus <span style="font-weight: 700;">have not yet crossed the midline</span>.</p></li></ol><div><br /></div><ol start="1" style="margin: 0px;"><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">The Impact:</span> A lesion in the left basis pontis interrupts these descending left UMN fibers. The right facial nucleus in the right tegmentum loses its main upstream drive.</p></li><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">Forehead Sparing:</span> Because the upper face portion of the right facial nucleus receives bilateral UMN input (from both the left and right hemispheres), the intact right hemisphere keeps the forehead moving normally. The lower face, relying strictly on the now-disrupted contralateral (left) tract, droops.</p></li><li style="margin: 0px;"><p style="margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px;"><span style="font-weight: 700;">Result:</span> A clean <span style="font-weight: 700;">contralateral UMN facial palsy</span> that mirrors the <span style="font-weight: 700;">contralateral hemiparesis</span> perfectly on the right side of the body.</p></li></ol></div></div><div></div></div></div><div><div style="min-height: 3rem;"><button style="border-color: currentcolor; border-style: none; border-width: medium; outline: none;"></button><button style="border-color: currentcolor; border-style: none; border-width: medium; outline: none;"></button><div><button style="border-color: currentcolor;
